title: I'm a Pastor's Wife. Here's Our Rules for Marriage
author: Heidi Tai
summary: Writing as a pastor's wife of more than fourteen years, Tai responds to a Netflix documentary about the death of Mica Miller by setting out, as a numbered list, the rules that govern her own marriage. Her framing move is to treat the documentary not as an aberration but as an illustration of how church leadership can be corrupted and how Scripture can be pressed into justifying violence at home, and she cites Australian intimate-partner violence figures to argue that there are many more cases inside churches than are named. Rather than arguing doctrine in the abstract, she offers the list as a concrete picture of what mutual love, respect and submission look like in practice. The rules run from mutual submission to Christ and to one another, through the priority of marriage over ministry and the qualification of elders, to the acceptance of a spouse's no, freedom of movement and friendship, financial security, consent in sexual life, and external accountability from mentors and counsellors. The piece is useful in the archive as a lay-level statement of what a safe Christian marriage looks like, written specifically against coercive control.
points: Tai's central claim is that the documentary's value lies in giving words and images to coercive control, a form of abuse that leaves no physical evidence.
She refuses to treat the case as an outlier, arguing that sin corrupts church leadership and that the Bible itself gets used to justify marital violence.
The list places marriage ahead of ministry and ties that ordering to the eldership qualification in 1 Timothy 3.
Several rules are deliberately concrete safeguards against control, including accepting a spouse's no, freedom to leave the house alone, and mutual consent in sexual life.
The final rules push against isolation, requiring trusted friends, mentors and counsellors as external input into the marriage.
quotes: I won’t retell the details, but I appreciate how the documentary puts words and images to coercive control—behaviours which can be difficult to identify since the abuse leaves no physical scars.
Her story exposes how sin corrupts church leadership, and how the Bible can be used to justify violence in Christian marriage.
As a pastor’s wife myself for over 14 years, I felt compelled to respond to the documentary by clarifying what the Bible actually says is a safe and godly marriage.
This list of our “marriage rules” is not exhaustive, but I hope it paints a picture of what mutual love, respect, and submission looks like in a marriage which seeks to honour Jesus.
This means biblical submission is never forced, but is voluntary, willing, and an expression of our respect for Jesus.
We put each other first, which means our marriage comes even before our ministry. An unloving, unfaithful, and neglectful husband is not qualified to lead a church.
We hear, respect, and accept each other’s “no”. Love is patient and kind, not hurried and coercive.
We invite external input and accountability into our marriage, from trusted friends, mentors, and counsellors. We will live in community and not be an isolated unit.
